It allows you a ton of segments to get it perfect um as opposed to that just one time through and so you know, we'll see how it comes out, but I told you the story, you know, we did it and then and then went back in and spent another 2 and 1/2 hours on it. cuz you want it to be perfect and and I think they're the best in the business at putting together something like that and you know, it's it's that old rule at a wedding, don't hand the microphone to anyone. You'll you'll just have a runaway mic and then the party will be over. So I understand the reason for that, you know, it's it's about the it's about the person going in and us hearing him um you know, talk about his journey and just to be a part of it is you know, obviously an honor. >> Coach, what after practice you sign autographs with with fans specifically? Can you guys tell me >> Well, Paul took me over there to find this kid who had a birthday. Now, I my understanding was he was going to be like over here and so I looked at PK and I'm like, all right, here we go. Um I mean, we're not just going to sign one, but someone had a birthday and and then 100 others had a birthday. >> In what area Shawn have you seen Troy Franklin make the most progress from the last year? >> His understanding the formations, the details, you know, maybe in a different offense where he's lining up outside right, you you know, now all of a sudden he's getting used to the different roles he's playing and the alignments on the field. He's got real good burst. But that would be the one thing, you know, he's comfortable within the framework. It's so much different than the system he had in college. >> Same question about Franklin. What have you seen him >> Yeah, really pleased with how he's doing. Um he's just one of those congested ball catchers, you know, his feet stay on the ground. So when receivers catch the ball with their feet on the ground, they're usually pretty good run after the catch. So you don't see him skipping in the air, jumping, you know, in in that that means he's got a lot of confidence, you know, in catching this thing the right way and and um I think in college this that final year, I think he had three walk-off touchdown, literally the last play of the game in cuts where he caught it and and didn't like he was full stride when he caught it. Um if you're breaking stride for a catch, there's that tick of a second everyone gets a little bit of leverage on you. So and he's he's extremely smart. Um Yeah, he's doing really well.

title: Spencer Fano and Joe Thomas hit it off! | Training Camp Insider
text: Welcome into Training Camp Insider presented by Gregory Industries. Nathan Zagura alongside the Hoff Joe Thomas Hall of Fame ceremony just down the way this weekend. And so we got to have the gold jacket in town. Hoff, it's great to see you. >> Hey, it's great to be here with you guys. And we had a real special practice out there today. >> Boy, did we. Yeah. No pads, but this was a day for the quarterbacks and in particular Hoff Deshun Watson and it was a day that was needed. >> Yeah, this is my first day of training camp, but reading the reports, hearing from you and the the great folks of Cleveland Browns daily, a little rough between the two quarterbacks, especially Deshun Watson last couple days, it was really a bounceback day. He was polished. He was shar and out of the huddle. operated clean in a bunch of different situations that a lot of times it can trip a young team up, especially an offense playing for this offensive coordinator for the very first time. And so, a lot of really positive things happened out here today. And Deshawn putting the ball where it needed to be opened up the possibilities for us to be able to witness some greatness out there at receiver. >> Yeah, which was fun. And that greatness is in the form of our young receivers, Denzel Boston, Casey Conpsion. They continue to do it. in particular off this was your first look at Denzel Boston and I got to tell you it's one of those things where we were excited on draft night obviously we were able to get him he's a guy the Browns considered had Casey been off the board they might have taken him at 24 and yet you get both of them in here but Boston the size it's what we've been looking for that big >> you've been calling for it for a long time >> oh baby boy have I sometimes my voice would get horse saying get me some weapons here but we've got them and and that's going to be fun >> yeah it was fun I mean they weren't in pads today so you weren't really able to see the full monty as far as what they can do at receiver. But there was multiple times that these receivers were catching the football in stride because the quarterback delivered it on time on the money and those guys would have been able to break an arm tackle and go the distance to the house. And so I think for Browns fans, your takeaway is this is what this offense could look like under Todd Monkin and it could be very exciting. >> Yeah. And that's all we want excitement because you know this defense is going to be very good. Now, the defense still at the defensive tackle position for the second straight day down five of those defensive tackles. There was no Mike Hall, no Mason Graham, no Malik Collins, no Kalia Davis, no Sam Kamara. So, guys that we just signed off the streets are are out here getting reps and and quite frankly, they're holding their own. So, that's good. But the story of the day, Deshun Watson on time. The arm looked live. The ball was kind of catching the receivers as opposed to the other way around. And that's when you know quarterbacks throwing it really well. Shore Sanders had an excellent day. Also, just an encouraging day for this offense. They'll be back in pads tomorrow. Hopefully, they can continue that momentum. Now, one of the things that you need, and the Hoff knows this very well. It's why he's wearing the gold jacket to have a good passing offense as a quarterback. You need time and you need the big guys up front to get the job done. Now, Spencer Fono and Dwan Jones, they have been rotating at left tackle. You know, Dwan's game, you got to meet Spencer earlier today. What did you see from those guys out there at the tackle position? >> Well, they were smooth today. They were clean, I would call it. You know, it's hard to say without pads on to really evaluate the job that they did. But you didn't notice them. And as an offensive tackle, that's the best thing anybody can say about me, right? Oh, I didn't even really notice that you were out there because that means you didn't notice the guy that I was blocking because he was eliminated. He was wiped off the screen. And uh Jared Verse had a nice day today when he had the opportunity, but Dewand and Spencer did a nice job keeping him away from the quarterback. There was no obvious mistakes out there. Both guys played solid. And it seems like today was that day where that offensive line came together a little bit. You started seeing some of that chemistry, those guys on the same page. Again, when the quarterback can make the play, that means you don't notice the offensive line because they're doing their job. >> Yeah. And really the one time Verse really made the big play in that four-minute situation at the end. That was a toss out. And Dwan was actually trying to get out in front of that. So that happened behind him. That happened behind him right there. Now Spencer Fono had a play today that was so exciting. It got George Warhop to sprint onto the field when he was out in front. Pulling made a nice block, allowed for a big gain on a run play. When you see that, you see George Warhop, you know him well. When you see him that fired up, what's that tell you? >> That means the boys are doing a good job because he's one of the toughest coaches I've ever been around. He's a tremendous offensive line coach. He was my mentor. Coached me for the majority of my formative years, I would say, in the NFL from years three through eight or so, somewhere in there. Um, and you can see already the mentality that he has, the tough, the physical, the hard-nose. You're seeing that on his players now. And that's exactly what you want as an offensive line coach. You want your players to embody your personality. And with George, we called him General George for a reason, right? And you're starting to see that nasty out of this offensive line. And that's just what Todd Mon wants to see up front. >> You got to have that. And we got to have something today that has been months in the making. The meeting of Joe Thomas and Spencer Fono. You guys got to sit down for an exclusive one-on-one interview. You are not going to want to miss this. And guess what? You don't have to because here it comes right now. I'm here with the Browns first round draft choice left tackle Spencer Fono. Spencer, thanks for being here today, man. >> Thank you for having me. Thank you. >> Yeah, this is really exciting. We were just talking off camera before we started, but when you were drafted, I was actually in El Salvador on a mission trip and I brought my Starling specifically so I could find out what was going on with the Browns draft. And after the draft, I heard you said some nice things about me and I was really excited to be able to try to FaceTime to welcome you to Cleveland. It didn't work. Schedules didn't align because after you've been drafted, you know how crazy things get. But it's great to be able to sit here next to you >> in person in Berea get to watch this afternoon. Yes, sir. >> You take the field for the very first time. >> Yes, sir. And this is crazy just like sitting next to one of my heroes right now. And so I don't know. It makes you're making me kind of nervous. >> Well, I'm doing my best to try to make you nervous, man. But [laughter] sir, >> you I'm sure you can handle it. Uh, three years in college at Utah. Started out as a left tackle. >> Yes, sir. >> Last two years playing on the right side, all-American, all the wards. You name it, you won it. Um, but now 21 years old, stepping up to the big leagues, first round draft choice for the Cleveland Browns. They're looking for the left tackle of the future. Um, exciting for me to be able to watch you out there on draft day. you said, >> "Hey, I'm happy that I don't have to block Miles Garrett because he's on my team." >> How did that turn out for you? >> Well, it looks like uh at least it's it's kind of true for this year, [laughter] but we'll see about next year. >> We'll see about next year. But the one thing I am really excited for, and I was thinking about it the night you were drafted, is my old offensive line coach, George Warhop, is here. He was my mentor. He's the guy that probably had more impact on my NFL career than anybody else. Now, he gets to coach you. What's that been like having George Warhop in those meeting rooms coaching you from day one as a rookie? >> It's been so cool. Um I feel like he just Yeah, he's like the perfect coach for me, especially at this point in time. Um just always whatever rep I have, he's telling me exactly what I need to do to get better um on every single rep. And so there's always something for me to work on. Um which is it's huge. And he's just so detailed and the things that he teaches work. So, um, getting better out here has been so much fun. >> He's going to grind you into the dirt, and that's one of the things that's kind of consistent all across offensive line coaches, but for you making that switch from playing the last couple years at right tackle now to left tackle. What's been the biggest adjustment making that switch right now? Um, I think the biggest thing is just you're so used to like pushing off of one leg to go in like a a certain direction or Yeah, I see. I think the biggest thing is just um building up though like those reps back up in my right leg of just getting out, you know, getting out of my stance faster. >> So, I had my right hip replaced last year because to your point, if you're a left tackle, all that weight is going through your right leg, right? And so that's the leg that ends up getting strongest and gets the most beatings. But George, I think, was one of the greatest offensive line coaches in the NFL for a long time. Still is because of the drill work that he did, right? The number of reps you're going to get, the way he strengthens that legs using sandbags and bands and bunggees and every apparatus you can imagine. But is there anything in particular that you've been doing out here to kind of help make that transition as quick and as easy as possible going to the left side? Honestly, I think it's um I'll just do the extra reps on my own and just whatever coach has me doing. Um every drill that he has just gives me more reps and yeah, he puts more strength into that right leg. Like you said, he has those uh those sandbags. >> Oh yeah, >> those sandbags that they'll get. >> They've been getting this leg real strong. >> I'm pretty old and kind of weak now. I don't even know if I could pick those things up anymore. [laughter] >> It's I bet you could. I bet you could. But it is that's probably the most burning >> 60 70 100 lbs. It's amazing. And one of the things I always appreciated, George really understood how to connect your feet to your hands and your body, right? A lot of it goes through your core. That's why you have to have that super strong core. And we always drilled tons of things to make sure we were overloading our core. We're overloading our legs and our feet and our hands and making sure we're always playing in balance. And that's one of the things I think he just continues to teach wherever he goes. And I'm excited to watch what you guys are able to put out there. Five new offensive linemen this >> Yes, sir. It's tough for any offensive line, much less a rookie now switching over to the other side. What's it been like playing with an entirely new group of offensive linemen? Not only for you, but just those guys finding a way to get on the same page as quickly as possible. >> Honestly, I feel like it hasn't like for me, I feel like it hasn't been really hard to work with the five new or four new guys. um just because everybody in the room was everybody is just such good dudes that all have like the same uh mentality and like the same goal in mind which is we want to be a damn good offensive line. Um and then we have leaders in the room like um we got like Titus Elton and Zion um guys that have a lot of experience that we kind of just see what they do and we follow their lead. Uh I feel like it's been really easy being behind those guys. >> Hank Freley was a big mentor to me when I was a rookie. He was our our starting center. Now he's the offensive line coach for the Detroit Lions. You may have interviewed with him at the combine possibly. Um who's been that guy, that veteran voice that's really kind of taken you under their wing and kind of helped show you the process of getting ready for a training camp pro uh practice and kind of the process that you need to go through on a weekly basis to get yourself ready for an NFL season. >> I feel like it really has been like those three that I mentioned like all three of them have been so helpful for me. I mean after practice every like almost every day I get some work in with Zion. Um he's showing me um like the like with his with his old team he was um he played with Slater. So he he would tell me kind of things that he would go through in his process. And then um every in the meeting room I sit right next to Titus where he's giving me tips um like all throughout the meetings and um just on yeah tips on what to do, what not to do. Um and then Elton. Elton has been really helpful because he was uh at Green Bay he was left tackle there for a little bit. >> He played at all in Green Bay. >> And then he was really been helpful for me like on that get off part of it where he's um telling me how he got his to his get off and what he did to improve on that. So those three have been awesome. some tips with you here over the next week that I'm very excited about to help with that get off because uh as I'm sure you've noticed already or maybe knew even coming into training camp, >> getting off the line of scrimmage as fast as possible is like the number one most important thing for a tackle in the NFL because those dudes are timing up the snap. And this is not news to anybody, but the guys that we play against are much faster, better athletes, and better looking than us. And so we got all right. Well, maybe not better looking than Spencer, but better looking than me. And we got to do everything we can to gain an advantage. >> And one of those things is we know the snap count and they don't. So getting off the line of scrimmage is so important. >> What have you noticed as far as that transition from the college game to the program specifically with pass protection that has been the biggest difference or the biggest change or the biggest adjustment? >> I think that's exactly what it is. The get off. I mean, um, these guys get off the ball so much faster than like anyone did in college. Um, so I think that's been the biggest adjustment. Like when in college when I was in a three-point stance, I felt like I could like still short set like anybody [laughter] there, but now it's like if I'm in three-point stance, I have to really make sure I'm getting out of there like straight back and getting into my set. Um, so I think yeah, just the get off has definitely been the the biggest difference. Right now you're playing left tackle and you're splitting reps with Dewan Jones. Yes, sir. >> Coming from college, you probably never came off the field, right? >> Starting as a freshman all the way through your junior season before you declared for the draft. text: Yeah, him missing a couple reps, you know, it's it's good to have him back um yesterday, but he did a nice job when he was in there. Um he's got really good athleticism. He's got strength. What just what have you seen from him and his progress? >> I love Bunk's play style. He's he's one like his mindset. He's got the right mindset. So, he's been doing a really good job communicating that with uh me and Matt and Coach Gatsy. And um yeah, so it's every day you're just kind of learning, you know, hey, I want to focus on this more. Just how he takes charge. Um, and just watching him obviously these last seven years has been pretty cool. What have you seen from like WY and DY and they're kind of in their second seasons now within the system? Yeah, I I think both of those guys have come along and taken a big step forward. Um WY uh he's he's a versatile player. He can play off the ball or on the ball. Uh Dabney's probably more of an onthe- ball guy, but he's still um taking a lot of steps forward and as he's improved as much as anybody over these first few days. Flores is going to throw a hell of a lot at you, too. >> How do you get to that elusive continuity with your offensive line when has Banks taken an 11 on 111 snap yet this camp? >> Yeah. I mean, obviously, you know, you have those guys, but like, yeah, there's always competition. We're we're these guys are out here. They're competing. John John's a cool guy just because coming out of Cincinnati, he was a a rocket aeronaut. He's a rocket scientist. We we call him in the room, but uh it's he's a super intelligent guy. Um he has a lot of versatility. He's been playing some tackle now. Obviously, he was been playing inside guard and center. Say uh Jordan Morgan breaks a chin strap or can't find his helmet uh as opposed to injury. >> Yeah. [clears throat] >> What exactly are you doing at left tackle if you don't have him? >> Yeah, I mean that's kind of where we got to figure it out over camp. Um is our next best option. You know, we have a few guys that we're working over there. Um so that's that's a big thing of what we have to figure out. >> [clears throat] >> Do >> you need to figure out your receiver depth start too? So, um it's it's been really fun to watch because those guys go out there with the right mindset every day. text: Hey, hey. Hey, hey, hey. hey, hey. D. Morning. >> Well, let's let y'all jump into it and uh start right away. Anybody got questions? >> Yeah. So, how do you get >> Can All right. Sorry. How do you get the bumps and the ups and downs kind of smoothed out so >> yeah I think anytime you have any young guy um whatever position it is there's going to be some ups and some downs. I think it's the consistency. When you come in and you look at the film, you talk to the guys, what are you working on technique-wise, what can you improve on? Is there some things that you're like, man, that was uh you just missed that when you hit the ball clean in his specific situation, or was it like, hey, that was a good hit, you know, um that was a bad hit. There's a difference when you look at a kicker. Um there's a good miss and there's a bad miss, you know, and it all depends on the contact they make when you really slow it down. Sometimes you can't see that when you're watching it live. Um you you'll see at practice I move around different spots during the field goal periods just looking at different things because there's different aspects when you're viewing it. Whether you're in front of the kicker, behind the kicker, to the side of the kicker, you're able to see different things. That's why we have all the camera views because you're looking at multiple things, right? Um, so you just got to have him be a consistent person every day he's here and just continue to improve on it because everything there's something to probably tweak or look at every day. Um, and you just want to see him get better and it's not so much the makes and misses right now. Um, it's more so about the ball contact is what I'm looking at. I don't think anyone probably should even out the learning curve on that. >> Well, I think that's unique for Green Bay and the practice fields to be honest with you. Um, and the stadiums I don't know even in my time in New England we dealt with a lot of wind at practice and even in Metife. First off, you're dealing with the wind dynamics and it's been really great for me um and him and all the specialists is when we go to practice, the wind is there, but when we go into Lambo and do walkters and stuff, honestly, I look at the wind there and I look at it at night and then we go in there, it's like, wow, you don't feel anything, you know? So, I don't put as much stock on the practice stuff as I will in the stadium stuff. um you know, even kicking in there in those elements because it's totally different. You know, a headwind 12 miles an hour outside with gust of 25 really feels like a light breeze almost inside, you know, whereas at practice you're out there and you're looking at the flags and it's moving and you're like, "Woo, it's a tough day to kick." So, it's good to have those. So, I think a lot of times at practice the results may not be what we want them to be or not as good as they could be or whatever may be, but putting guys in tough situations, kicking into that into it and then going inside and seeing it's not as windy as it's going to be. Um, so I think at practice I think it's really good that we do have the wind we have um whether it's the northeast, southeast and going different directions and then we have the indoor, right? So, it's coming off and it's actually different, you know. Um, and that's what goes through learning the ball, learning how the what, when's playing every day. Um, so I would say like I'm going to put more stock into game days and stuff like that. And then when we kick in stadiums, you know, um, I think that's where it's going to the growth of it is is he contacting the ball better, you know, it's not so much is he hitting the ball and we're nine for nine, whatever, you know, or we were three for four. I've been around kickers and went n for nine, had a terrible day. When you look at the film the next that day, you're like, "Ah, I really didn't hit the ball good." They went three for four or whatever or three for five and it's like, "Well, at least you struck the ball well and we knew we were missing." So, it's a lot of when you watch the film where it was, but obviously in the stadiums working together, you hope obviously you're making more kicks there. But I think there's more value in that than what we're doing on the practice field. >> Robski from ESPN. Um, Matt said the floor said yesterday that Trey likes the ball. a little differently than Brandon did maybe and you know Daniel's obviously got to adjust to that. How does he like it held? >> So here we go. >> Oh, this is going to be awesome. So each kicker is different, right? Everybody see right? >> Um this is my football. All right. But each kicker is different and it all depends on how to strike the ball. But playing win and elements and stuff like that and again a lot of guys like the ball straight up and down. Everybody with me on this? Okay. All right. However, when you're playing in wind, and it also depends on where the wind's in your face, right to left, left to right, right? So, if you want to drive the ball through the wind, I move, you have to lean it forward a little bit. Okay? So, most guys that kicking whether have forward lean. Now, after that, it depends on whether it's left or right, whether I'm going to slightly lean it into me or it's just a forward lean with no lean into the holder. So like Daniel's out there and we're talking and we're doing the win. It's like hey we're just going ball down a little forward here or the next day maybe hey balls down but also slightly into you a little bit. So each kicker is different but what you work on more when you play element stuff is a little bit more forward lean and then it may be straight and it may be into it. Okay. What that allows and some kickers actually have like into them small into them big. Okay. Two different into the lead. That's where like Daniel working with him, it's here and it's into small, medium, whatever it may be. Because what happens with the kicker is it allows him by adjusting the football to not actually change their swing. You're moving the football and the lean. So when the guy goes to actually kick the ball and make contact, he's making the same contact and he's letting the lean of the football do the work for him. So there's that's a lot of the stuff we're working with in practice and that's what's really good about our practice field is because the wind is going to be so different every day. Does that make sense? So like now it's a lean into out to and now we're working together and the more rest we can get out there in that wing is it's going to really help us. Is that >> I couldn't. >> Okay. All right. All right. No problem. mention the athletic I haven't been here as long as some of these other guys but I've never seen a coach wear cleats at practice and I I asked this seriously like where did have you been doing that for a long time and what benefit do you get out of that? Have you had a chance to talk to former kickers like Brian Longwell and Mason Crosby about what to expect in Lambo? >> I I haven't I haven't personally talked to Mason or anything like that. title: Nick Sorensen: "It Always Starts With Me" | Dallas Cowboys 2026
text: This guy Calvin Watkins Dallas wanted to use. What's the biggest adjustment that you needed to make from after what happened last year to going into camp this year for your for your unit? >> The adjustments? I think the main thing for us is just our return game, focusing on that. I think the big thing that showed up was penalties, so we've made a big emphasis of, you know, how we place our hands, how we got to finish with our feet. So, we want to be better in the in the penalty aspect of it. And I think that's going to be have a huge, you know, a huge impact on our return game cuz we had some big returns to get called back and those end up being huge huge yard losses. So, I think it start It's just It goes back to those fundamentals. >> Personnel you had or just how you were teaching it or just a combination of the two? >> I think it's a combination of everything and then, you know, it always starts with me and and how we teach, how we stress, how we correct, and then we got to apply it. >> All right, so deal with Scott Bull. There's so much talk about Blue and Moffitt with their doing at running back. Can you talk about the impact they need to make and how you could use them on special teams that they could make this work? >> It's huge. I think they both have to have an impact on special teams. They're different type body types and the type of players in the positions that they'll play on special teams, so it's really how can they carve out that niche for us and produce? You know, I think Blue is more we trained him in both spots of being a PP and actually played a game of PP last year, but I think he has the ability to be a good gunner. He's also in the return game. We move Phil in some more interior positions where Blue would be more of an outside guy, but I think in their own way it's more about being consistent and producing daily and just continuing to get better because special teams is still new to both of them. >> Well, Blue could be a returner, but you have Perine, you know, and so his size, you know, what other outside of gunner, what else can he do to help you guys on special teams? >> Like I said, it could be punt return. There are certain spots on kickoff return he can do. You put two returners back there. And then really it's more matchups on the if he was going to be in the front line of kickoff return. It's not that he can't do that. He's got He's got to pass protect also and block big guys that are rushing the quarterback, too. So, he has that ability. And then obviously Gunner, and he has also played PP for us. So, we're we're moving him to a lot of a few different spots to see where he can have the most success. >> Nick Alvarez with ESPN. CJ was a guy who was around for a long time and pretty influential in your room. Who's kind of taking over that a little bit for you or is anybody taking over that? >> I think it's I think it's been by committee right now. You know, I think we've we've got guys that are still really young, but that have done a lot of cool things for us like, you know, a Flow and, you know, Brevin, um, Marist, even Shammar James did well last year as a rookie. I mean, there's And Marquis has been around, so we added PJ Lock who's who's been in the league a while. So, I think it's more by committee right now. I think CJ was kind of established as that guy, you know, that's been the leader and been the old head. We've got a good like mixture of guys that I think are sort of in that mid-20s age range to where they're, you know, comfortable, but they're also bringing up the young guys and the young guys could step up, too. So, it's it's kind of been by committee and I think it's been cool to see them challenge each other. >> Okay, it looked like Aubrey was working on a dirty kick off. I don't know what you guys call it, like a knuckleball kind of thing. Is that something you you guys want to add to his uh arsenal on the kickoff? >> Yeah, I think it's a something everyone kind of toys with. >> Cam Show with The Athletic and the Falcons. DeShawn Barham. Uh, Marquis kind of stood out on defense with what what he brings to the football team. What do you see? >> Well, he's got everything that you would think would produce on special teams too. Sides, speed, he's aggressive. Um, he's physical. So, it's Again, for rookies the biggest thing is it's totally different. Some of them didn't even do much special teams. If they did, it was usually early in their career. And punt's different, punt return's different, kickoff's different, kickoff return's different. But, how fast can he just apply it? So, we try and make it as simple as possible so the guys can play fast and just be football players. Put him in a spot that he can just be himself and play fast and aggressive and make plays. >> And then having a veteran punter like like a Bryan Anger, just how does that help you in your job? >> Yeah, it's been huge. I think I think I probably have the best group of specialists in the league. I'm I've been fortunate. Same thing I felt last year with all three of them. It's it's incredible. They're really close. They're really smart and they're pros and they do everything that makes it a lot easier for me. >> Nick Eatman, Cowboys Radio 105.3 The Fan. Uh putting together special teams in preseason is a special kind of fun, intended, special kind of challenge. How much, when you start doing that next week, are you trying to get guys on the field and how much are you doing it with plan in mind for who you want to see when the season's coming? >> It's You're right, it does take a lot of planning. One, you got to see who's healthy cuz, you know, you're doing a lot of practices. You get these joint practices. Some guys get banged up, so you want to be smart there. Some guys aren't playing. They may play more on offense or defense. So, it's not just who plays, it's when they play, too. We don't want to overload them in certain quarters or have them, you know, not loose. It's it's kind of piecing it together, but you got to get guys reps so you can actually evaluate them. And that's that's what's been big on some of these days that we first get these pads on that we try and create some competitive drills that we can evaluate and have a winner and loser. And then you get that with the joints. That's why I like that we have two joints this year cuz that's a it's a big opportunity that we can see our guys compete. That adds reps that are like game reps. Thank you. >> Nick Harris, Fort Worth Star-Telegram. With KaVontae Turpin, we've seen him do some work as PR. What have you seen from him and just the trust that he's picked up from you guys with >> Probably a lot of the same thing everybody says. He he's picked it up really quick. Um he's catching punts, too, cuz you know he's he's done that in college. He didn't have a whole lot of them but he had two for touchdowns. He didn't do it his last year. So, with all the young guys we got to train these guys up to be ready and he's been great. He's he's smart. He picks it up really quick. Make the communications, runs the huddle well and always gives great effort. So, he's he's done everything we've asked for so far. >> Hey Nick, Patrick Walker DallasCowboys.com. As the special teams coordinator you have a lot of curve balls coming your way. C.J. Goodwin uh Goodwin retiring. Um you have the injury to Princeton Fan, Elijah Clark. Thankfully doesn't look like his is going to be serious but you have all of this coming at you plus guys like Ryan Flannigan. Maybe you don't have as much access to him nowadays because of his value. Just talk about the challenge of trying to piece that that special teams unit together over the course of training camp and preseason. What do those conversations look like from your standpoint going into the regular season? >> That's a good question cuz I love that part of it. That's the part to me that's exciting. I mean with you mentioned Flo, that happened last year too. I mean he ended up starting and getting, you know, couple hundred yard games I believe it was where we couldn't use him as much. So, you're that's why you got to train so many guys in different spots and continue to stress, you know, being ready to go. Whether it's a practice squad guy, you can always access that information you're that you gained in preseason or in or in off season. You're just always training guys. You're always getting them potentially ready to go to two different spots. He's always got to think ahead and that that part is fun. It is a challenge but that's part of the special teams where someone all of a sudden becomes a starter. Now you don't have him of, you know, as available as much. I mean it happened with Hunter when he had a lot more reps to one or two games to where we we're just going to keep him on punt rather than being on three or four phases. So, that's continuous. It is fun. It is a challenge but that's our job and that part is it's fun to do. I like it. >> Thanks guys. >> Thanks.

title: Christian Parker: "We Want to Play With Violence and Physicality" | Dallas Cowboys 2026

So on the blackboard, it looks one way, but in in principle on the field, it looks another. So just getting those guys as much exposure to both type of spots as possible with the different calls, different formations that we know we're seeing is the most important thing right now. >> Todd Archer with ESPN, you mentioned embracing the play style. Yeah, I think that, you know, the first thing is we want to be um we want to be detailed in our work um and our fundamentals and technique and obviously the mastery of the scheme. Um but there's an element of of violence and physicality that we want to play with that we will play with. So I think it's just kind of tying all those things together in terms of knowing your job, knowing what the man next to you is doing, who are you connected to, are you on an island on that certain play? Um and then doing that with a with an attitude um and the physicality required to play this game. >> Then next week practice against the Rams. Shotty told us the starters aren't going to play in the preseason. What's the importance of these practices seeing another team uh even if it's not, you know, taken to the ground football? >> Yeah, I think it's real important, especially um you know, as much um experiences as coach McVey has and and and Matthew Stafford at that position, you know, the pre-nap looks and the motions and the things they do formationally. They've been a very successful offense during his tenure there. Um, so it's going to be a good test for us to, you know, where we're at and make sure our eyes are right and and we're playing with the right uh demeanor. >> With the athletic bone rebell, we seen him the other day get some pass breakups, some pads come on. What's the what's the next step for him? >> I think the next step for him is just making sure that um he's able to to live on in a single play. And what I mean by that is, okay, what's the split here? What's the situation? What am I defending with a certain play call? um because he has all the physical attributes. So everything with him now is just working on everything from the neck up and just make sure that we're thinking the game properly. And that's a that's a quick, you know, two or three second assessment because once you're getting in your stance and you're ready to play ball, you want to play with a clear mind. Um so just being able to do that and just finish plays. But he's doing a good job is he's he's extremely hardworking. Um he's extremely willing. He wants to be coached. He runs towards that. So uh we're really excited about how he's progressing with everything we're doing so far. And then kind of the same thing but with Jan Barham. >> Yeah, Jan is uh you know, we had a vision for him when we drafted him. Um and that's coming to life. You know, I think he brings a certain physicality and demeanor to the inside of the defense and you feel that. Um so same thing with him. Any any young player, you're at a different level, you know, so the the offensive information, how the play style is, the rules of the game, all those different things. It's a constant educational approach when you have young players. So you want to allow them to keep it simple and clean to play fast by also kind of elevating their knowledge of the game, you know, so we can execute and maximize each call. >> Joe Hoy, Dallas Morning News. Kind of on that note, um you obviously had a lot of sex success with the guys in Philly, the young guys, um obviously pass Denver, getting these young guys ready to go quickly. What goes into that? >> Uh it's a lot. I think you you want to number [clears throat] one be as detailed as you can, but also make it simplistic for them and and do things in buckets so they can, you know, compartmentalize the information that you need them to know. Um, everybody has learned a playbook at some point in their career, right? And some college defenses are more advanced from a sense of volume and things like that than than they are in the NFL in some instances. So, the difference is the level of detail. He doesn't have they don't have to worry about study hall and, you know, doing those things that college students have to do anymore, you know, if they still have to do them anyways now. But um you know they don't have to worry about those things. So then it's the the NFL 101 as we call it. You know what are the rules? You know there's going to be a DB in every preseason game. You know every year not every preseason game but every year in the preseason you know receiver catches the ball he doesn't get touchdown. You know so those uh NFL 101 principles formation awareness situational awareness field awareness all of those different things that it takes to play the NFL style game. you want to advance that with them so then they can play with a clear mind and focus on their detail and fundamentals uh schematically. >> It seems like it's coming to life a little bit with Caleb and Jan and Malachi too. Um how much also credit goes to them for being quick learners and getting up to speed as much as they have so far? >> Yeah, I think a lot of it does. I think that's something that we really assess in the draft process you know um we can you know really um assess that in that process and I think our staff is doing a phenomenal job with those guys as well. I mean, the the time they put in um individually with those guys and also in the meeting room to get them up to speed. Um they're working extremely hard and and really uh taking a collaborative approach in terms of uh you know, kind of shortening the curve for those guys. >> Tommy, Dallas Cowboys.com. Christian, you've talked about how important communication is for you and this defense. How have you seen your players buy into that and communicate early on here? >> Yeah, I mean, I think if you step in our meeting room and you hear how loud it is, you might think something wrong is going on. And that's a good thing. you know, guys are understanding what what needs to be said. And I think, you know, communication is two parts, right? So, it's giving and receiving. So, I can't just be aimlessly yelling and saying a bunch of things if I don't know who I'm talking to, what those words mean, how that changes things, when we can adjust something, when we can't. Um, so I think they're taking that next step in terms of who am I speaking to, and also if I'm receiving that communication, I got to make sure my ears are open. I need to know who I'm listening for. But, uh, they're definitely taking that to heart. Um, we still have a, you know, more to go, but, uh, there's a lot of encouraging things that are happening from a vocal standpoint. >> And specifically on Caleb, how have you seen him embrace his first NFL training camp? And what have you made of the work he's done at Nickel and at safety? >> Yeah, I think he's embraced it the from what we expected. You know, he's uh he's very willing. He's very curious. And I think that, you know, going to the previous question, curiosity is is one thing for young players that you really look for. They want to know the why behind everything. we give them that upfront, the intent behind each thing that we're trying to do. Um, and so I think with him, he has that natural spirit about him. Um, for sure. And I think that he's managing both positions well. You know, we kind of have a certain plan for him each day in terms of how that looks. We do that for every player. Um, but he's really uh embracing, you know, what we're trying to do with him and and overall as a defense. >> Coach Sydney Staples, DJ10 Sports. We've been told by players, coaches alike, that you're a really good teacher. Who are teachers and coaches of your past and I mean school football regardless that you kind of pull from in any way? >> Yeah. Um I think you know going back to college I think uh you know Dr. Ernest McGawan he was my campaigns and elections teacher my junior year and um you know I think the way he compartmentalized information and taught me was real important. Um I think you know my parents as well. My mom was really hard on me from an academic standpoint. So, you kind of learn the importance of uh learning progressions and and teaching progressions as well, coming from her and and my dad, too. Um, I think coaching wise, you know, I've been around a lot of really good ones, I think, that have coached me number one, but I've also been able to coach with um, you know, so from, you know, Latrell Scott and and and Mike London and um, Bob Trot, um, Brandon Streer, some of those guys, they were always detailed. They always had a plan and it was an an order of operation in terms of how you learn. Zomb Burden is another one from when I was a player. Um and then I think as a coach when you get to that next level um in the NFL you have so much more time to do that and you can get more creative because you're dealing with adults who don't have to worry about algebra and you know geometry and earth science and all that like they're worried about football. So, um, Jerry Gray and Jason Simmons and Ed Donatel and obviously Vic Fangio, um, Clint Hurt. There's been a lot of I'm missing a lot of them, but there's been a lot of highle teachers I've been around. And I think that, you know, part of teaching is knowing where your student is and then trying to elevate him. So, you want to understand how they learn best. Is are they a walkthrough guy? Well, then you need to go outside or stand them up in the meeting room. Um, do they like studying on their own? Do you need to give them more material so they can do stuff by themselves? Is it a cahoot quiz that they can take in a limited amount of time or do they need to feel a little pressure? Um, do they put them in front of a classroom so they feel that, you know, from their teammates? It's different ways to do it and reach them and you want to try to be as diverse with the teaching style as possible so it's hitting the brains of each student in the room. >> Is there any specific player you think has a similar leadership style to you? >> Um, we'll wait to answer that. We haven't been in the fire yet. >> Coach Candace Lamb, D210 Sports. Jan Barum, seeing him being on the inside and then flexing to the outside here at practice, how important and how is his processing speed as a rookie here at camp? Um, I know he played a bit of both at college, mostly in the middle, but just being able to play here at that level. What has that been like? >> Yeah, I think the the point you made about him playing both is is one of his uh cheat codes that he has. you know, he's played equal amount of snaps almost at Maryland and Michigan, so he's been exposed to it. So, it's not like he he's seeing things that he hasn't seen before from that perspective sighteline wise. Um, I think that he is a fast processor and again, he's one of those young guys who's very eager to learn. You know, he wants to know the details. We try to keep it clean for those guys so the jobs aren't too different. It's just a different way of doing it, different alignment to do it. Um, but he has the right mindset to attack that at multiple positions and we've been real happy with his progress and his demeanor. Uh you have a rotation of pass rushers. How is What did you like about James Houston? Because he was the guy that was here last year that play got five sacks or whatever it was. What do you like about him? >> Yeah, James has a lot of just natural pass rush ability. You know, he's low cut. Um you know, he's not, you know, tall, but he has a long torso. He's low cut, so he can make those moves. He can get his foot in the ground and make counters very quickly. Um he's very aggressive to rush and for his size, he does have a physical capacity to him. So, um we like his urgency. You know, I think that's the one thing that we try to emphasize that get off on the ball. Um, you know, closing that space between you and the tackle or you and the guard, whoever's blocking you on that given play is critical in terms of making them uncomfortable and he already has that mindset. And I think the job that Chid and BT and Marcus and Brim are doing with those guys in terms of their mentality um, in terms of rushing as a unit is really important. So, all those guys are kind of falling in line with that. >> You talked about the communication and what it's like in the room and it can get loud. Can you kind of take us a little bit? Is it you show a play and you want everybody like you're showing emotion, you want everybody talking and >> Yeah. You know, if we're showing a play from practice, for example, if you're a linebacker on the field, you're making the front adjustment. You know, if you're outside linebacker and you see that the Y is off, you're saying something to your partner. If I'm a DB, I'm calling out the coverage communication. Motion happens. We're alerting this. We're we're passing off this. Once the play starts, what is that communication? We want the meeting room to sound the same as it does on the field. You know, your brain doesn't know when you're not taking a physical rep. It just knows that your brain is strained. So, as many reps that we can get on task as that as possible, we want to try to take advantage of those uh in that space. >> Yeah. Sean's talked a couple of times about uh your trash talk. Yeah. Can you just talk about that? And I know Kobe Ranch said you help give them an attitude on giving. Talk about why that's necessary, why you do that to the offense. >> Uh I think I'm just being myself, but we'll we'll uh we'll leave what's said on the field. >> One other thing. Um so much talked about. Can you talk about your sisters and how they are extensive to you? You brought Big Jordan in, you know, secondary coach, Ansley, all those guys. How they extended to you and what you like about them, >> man. It's uh it's been great. I think the the process we were able to go through from square one in terms of of hiring the staff was the right one. We were very thorough in the approach. Um starting with Marcus Dixon. You know, I was with Marcus for two years in Denver. Um you know, obviously he's a former player here. Um but Marcus is is a guy that I've been in the trenches with. I've stood side by side with Marcus when I was the DB coach there as well. So phenomenal teacher. Um he has a great level of detail. He brings an energy and attitude to that Dline room which is required. Um and he's doing a great job with that. Um Chadera Uzo Derebe coming from the college ranks, but he's a guy who's his name has been floating around for a couple years as a guy who's highly respected and all the Georgia guys I was with in my previous stop always spoke highly of him. You know, from Nolan Smith to Nico Dean and all those guys. Um and Chid has done a really good job adjusting to the game. some of the things they did schematically with with Kirby down there is very similar to what we do. Um so, you know, he's been able to kind of make that leap pretty seamlessly. Um Scott Simons, you know, known him um loosely for a couple years when he was the DC at Liberty and I was a GA at Texas A&M. Um and Scott's obviously a local product, but you know, his level of detail and also he has a experience as a play caller. He's called plays for I think about seven years between Liberty um and SMU. So, you know, he's getting a different scope. you know, he can widen the scope, but he can also tighten it down, and he's able to contribute in that manner with those guys. And that's a room that, um, we felt just getting more young development in there, and he's been very critical to that. Um, Derek Ansley, um, is a guy I've had a lot of respect for. You know, DA when I was a young coach, when he was the DB coach at at Alabama, you know, I'm trying to figure out like how he got there, like what was his track record, you know, and and being around him and getting to know him the last couple years. We were in division in the um AFC West before when he was with LA and I was with Denver. Um, but he's done a great job just establishing the brand of football and uh planting the flag in that in that manner. Um, you know, so he's he's done well. Ryan Smith, known Smitty since college. Um, and he's always been somebody I've trusted at a very high level. We've always talked about working together. Um, and I think that his exposure at the college game from Penn State to Elon to JMU to then going to Arizona, Virginia Tech, Northwestern, he's been around a lot of different schemes similar to what we do in the 34 structure. Um, so getting him with the safeties, he's a high level communicator as well. We have a bunch of great communicators on the staff. Um, and he's doing well, uh, in that capacity too. And then I think, you know, BT has had a lot of exposure the past couple years working with high level rushers and, um, bringing his expertise to the table has been been really good. And I think our young coaches too, and I I say young um, they're the same age as me, so you know, I'm not trying to say that the wrong way, but uh, from Rob Muschamp, you know, he had experience with DA from Tennessee. Um, he's been with the Chargers the past couple years. He's worked in the front, he's worked in the secondary. Um, he adds a lot of value to that room as well. Um, JJ Clark was the one holdover from last year's staff. JJ's also been a previous coordinator when he was at UTP. So, JJ has another guy in the middle of the defense. You want guys who were tied into the run and the pass who can widen that scope for the players and teach them the game in that manner. And he's been very valuable. Um, and Demetri Brim. Um, we got Brim from UCF. Um, so actually he has a lot of experience with Malachi. we were able to get kind of an inside track on on how Malachi was on the dayto-day, but um Brim has been a guy who who's been contributing at a high level as well with Marcus. He's his right-hand man. So, you know, from top to bottom, we felt like, you know, we knocked it out the park with a lot of these guys. There's a lot of first round draft picks on the staff. Um and it's been really fun to work and collaborate with them. We try to have a collaborative approach with everything that we do. um and the contributions from all of those guys in their different ways from tackling circuits to takeaway circuits to, you know, how we're, you know, setting up different fronts and tying everything together. Um, they've been a great addition. Um, and they've been a great help to me, you know, the first time doing this. >> Christian Adam Rosell with Spectrum News. I'm sure you had a vision and a plan for how you wanted to run a camp as a defensive coordinator, but 10 days in, maybe quick self-reflection on how it's matched those expectations or or how it's gone. Yeah, I think uh you know you have a vision for it and I think everything goes off the head coach, right? And I think Shotti and Tyler Bulls and Ryan Feeder and the way that we've been able to uh organize everything. I had all the the schedules and everything in the spring. So I was able to spend some time this summer um trying to organize everything and then make sure that we were three four days ahead. How we spending, you know, the days like today when we're not on the grass as a staff and with the players, how we spending the players off days as a staff in terms of planning ahead and doing those things. So, um, I think everything has gone, you know, pretty according to plan once we kind of got those schedules and figured out how we can, you know, divide the labor up as a staff and and with our time meeting wise and everything else on the grass. Um, it's been pretty good. Thank >> you. Thank you.

title: Klayton Adams: "Let's Play Winning Football" | Dallas Cowboys 2026
text: How's everybody doing? >> How are you? >> Super. I'm doing great. >> It's good. >> Pretty good weather. >> Beautiful. >> Calvin Watkins, Dallas Morning News. You were calling the plays the other day at practice. Just your thoughts of getting used to doing that for obviously down the line when the opportunity presents himself presents itself to you. >> Yeah, it was it was awesome. Um, I really I really came away from it uh feeling feeling good and just just the way that I felt like I made progress. Um, there were a lot of things that, you know, just going into that situation. I haven't done that very much. So, you're nervous about I don't want to call this backwards or I don't want to uh call the protection wrong or, you know, call something in the wrong area. And I I felt really good. I felt like I was able to get into a flow and um you know there's plenty of things that I want to do better but uh it felt like a really good step forward for me. >> What's one of those things you want to do better? >> Uh I want to know where CD Lamb is uh lined up better than I did. Uh cuz there's times where I'm, you know, calling some stuff for him and I'm like where's he where's he going? Uh so yeah, I got to do a better job of of kind of knowing where he's going to be based on that. We're not in a game plan mode right now. And so that was something that I didn't think about when we went into it is is I was just expecting him to be kind of at the point of attack on a lot of passes and and he went and lined up where he was supposed to. >> Clarence Hill DLS Cowboys look like Dax's put a little pressure on you by calling off Gotti. What does Gotti mean to you? Greatest offense there is. >> Uh I think it's amazing because to me it's just a standard that they've set for themselves. you know, it's something that's very easy for me if we're not having a great walkthrough or we don't have a great practice to pull that out and say that guys that's not what that is. So, um I don't think it's as much of like oh a numbers thing or you're going to rank here or you're going to do this or you're going to do that or you're going to be the greatest show on turf or any of these other things. To me, it's just like we want to be the best. You better freaking act like it every single second. Uh and you better hold yourself to that standard. And we can't be going to a walkth through with one foot out the door because it's an off day the next day or we can't the the foot needs to be on the floor of the car the entire time. And so I I love it. >> As good as y were last year, obviously there were you need to improve on. Can you talk about the what do you need to do better offensively than you did a year ago? >> Well, I just think one of the things that you always have to figure out when you're going into another year is how do you evolve? And the answer to that, I think it comes to you. It's not like you can just dig it out of the dirt. And so some of that we just got to work on and we got to keep, you know, finding it as we get holes poked in the things that we do and uh see how teams evolve on defense. Um I know that one of the things that I've challenged myself to is like how do we play winning football? Um, and as I've gotten older and grown into like higher level leadership positions, to me it's a little bit less about the numbers and and how how do you just, you know, put attack in the winkh home. And I think that we're set up to do that now with the way that we operate. Uh, let's let's play winning football. Let's do the things that it takes to ensure that we win. >> Clayton Todd Arch with his um shotty yesterday said you know there's not going to be a rotation that left eye has performed well. Obviously availability has been an issue for him. You have yesterday happened where he's going to be the guy and then he has the elbow thing. Is there anything that kind of says ah okay what you know can we can we get past this at all? >> Um yeah I mean I it sounded to me like the I'm not a doctor but it sounded to me like the elbow thing was just something that they wanted to look at. I don't think it was, you know, anything that was serious. But, um, yeah, I mean, I I think we want that for all the guys is to stay out there and try to develop as good a continuity as we can and and you know, like we're we're evaluating and trying to make decisions day by day based on what we're seeing. And part of being a great competitor is being able to do it every day. And so, if we're seeing good things, then we're going to keep the continuity in the group. If if it feels like there's a dip or there's an issue with availability, then, you know, then we need to roll guys. And so, um, the first casualty of war is the plan, right? And so, we go into the camp saying, "This is what's going to happen and things go a little bit differently and we have to pivot." I'm totally good with that. You know, I sometimes you got to reserve the right to change your mind. >> With Javante, obviously had a great first year with him. Is there a there more things that you think or you know what he likes now, whereas last year you kind of figured it out as the year goes along. Is there more that you can do with him in the run game or is he specific like you know these runs he does well? >> Uh yeah, I mean I think obviously uh the guy is pretty good on direct runs and he's hard to get down behind the line of scrimmage, but I think that he is a more diverse runner than he probably gets credit for. Um I think the guy does a really nice job with some of the outside zone stuff, particularly the weak side. He's got really quick feet. uh he's able to get in and out of cuts really well and and he's one of those dudes that's not scared to run through the smoke and that's what you're going to have to do um on some of the what some people would call mid zone which I don't believe in. I don't think it exists but some people call it that. Um I think he's good at I think he's good at a lot of things. >> Yeah. >> And John Mto with the athletic uh with Jaden Blue from last year to this year. Where would you say you've seen the most growth with him? Uh, I mean, you know, so far it's been consistency, which is really what we were looking for last year was to get a professional every day and, um, I think he's had, uh, some growth in those areas. Um, you know, I try to make sure that I talk to him every day and give him some feedback on what I think he's doing good and what he's not doing good and try to make sure that, you know, some of these guys are 22, 23, 24 years old. And so I just think having to having the ability, you know, which not everybody does, to have like adults on your roster to say, you know, like you think Dak would do that, you know, how do you think that that that he's carrying out his day? How do you think he prepared to show up uh today is is a very positive thing for us. And so those are the the things that we just got to continue to grow and look for. And so far uh there's been a lot of growth. kind of the same question, but for Ryan Penoy, you know, going back to that week five game where he kind of broke out, at least to us, against the Jets to now where he your guys number three, where have you seen him grow? >> Yeah, I he's one of those guys that came into the NFL kind of as an adult maturity-wise. Um, where he's grown is just uh instincts and understanding the game. And he's he's a fun player because he totally understands nuance. And so when you just start with a scheme, you have to make it as black and white as you possibly can so you can go hold the guys accountable. When guys are get to the, you know, the point where Flo is at in his career where, you know, it's kind of like he's he's uh developed consciousness, right? He understands this is why we're putting that in. And so that's, you know, one of the best things he does is he just he gets it, you know. >> Nick Harris for Star Telegram. the luxury of having that interior trio of uh Tyler Smith, Cooper BB, and Tyler Booker. Feel like last year it was like, "Yeah, it's going to be great, but Booker's a rookie, and now he's stepping into year two. Obviously, he has high expectations for himself." How have you guys been able to experiment just with a more mature trio of those guys? >> Uh, yeah, I mean, obviously the continuity in there is really good. Those guys do a really good job of communicating. Um, I'll tell you, it's been fun watching Sparks fly with those guys in the interior that we have on defense because those guys are big and thick and do a nice job over there, too. So, um, I think that the the best thing for those guys is that some of the absolute best interior players that we're going to see all year are on our team and we get to practice against them every day. And so, you know, there's times where we're able to say like, "Hey, I told you you can't do that against somebody who's an elite player." Because they get to practice against him every day. George Piggin experimenting with moving him around. Where is that in the evolution of things for the offense? >> Yeah, I mean to me it's a little bit more of like game plan type thing and then every once in a while we throw something in there and say, you know, how comfortable is he doing this? How comfortable is he doing that? You know, right now you sprinkle it in and then you figure out whether it's something that you can do full-time or not. >> Joe White, Dallas Morning News. Last year you talked about the communication level with the offensive line, getting to a point where they don't have to actually verbally communicate and they just know. Where are you guys from an offensive line standpoint with that and how do you go about kind of testing that and ascertaining whether that's where you're at? >> Yeah, I mean it is a hard thing to test because you in a walkthrough you want to hear it when you're standing from behind. So it's not something that's going to get encouraged. Uh but you can feel when they hit that level. Uh it's usually to me it ends up happening in sidelines uh on the sideline during games of hey I'm going to say this you know and you're not having to encourage them to do things. Um, with young players, it's difficult. You know, I think when you get when you get the older guys, obviously that's a little bit easier to do with some of the things that we're doing to try to invol evolve. It hasn't really been a priority right now. Um, that was something that when I was a line coach, I used to like to do an evening walkthroughs. All right, we can't say anything here. I'm going to give you the play. Everybody's got to know what they're doing. >> And then joint practices coming up with the Rams and the Saints. from just an offensive line standpoint and just where you want to do from a limma standpoint. How big will that be? >> Yeah, I think it's going to be great anytime you get the opportunity to test your metal against uh another team is is a good opportunity. So, obviously uh both of those teams have pretty good fronts that that have a lot of high picks on them and it'll be a great test for us. Tommy Yarcowboys.com. You mentioned earlier that Christian Parker when he was going through the hiring process, you got to sit in those meetings and hear from him about, hey, this is some of the things I noticed about your offense last year as you've had more of those conversations. How much has that helped you when you plan for the second year of this offense? >> Yeah, it's great because uh we have a year of this offense on tape now and you know, we've got a bullseye on our back. every time we take the field, people are going to want to measure themselves against us. And so, it's not going to be the same old stuff. It wasn't the same old stuff when we got to the end of the year last year. You know, people did a good job of trying to poke holes in what we do. And and that's to me is uh when you can really get to a very high level as a football team is when you got you got the other side of the balls knocking the ball back across the net and they're poking holes in what you do and forcing you to adjust because we're going to see anything that that we see at practice that's giving us problems. I promise you somebody else knows how to do it. And so being able to develop some of those answers right now is huge. And they've done a great job of that for us. >> And then what do you make of your two quarterbacks that are dug it out for a backup job and Joe and Sam? >> They're both doing an unbelievable job. Um and it it really is a testament to how important competition is. And um you know uh Joe's calling plays a lot cleaner than he has in the past. He understands pass protection a lot better than he has in the past. and and being here a year obviously with the terminology has been really good for him. And then you look at Sam who's a guy that started I think he started 17 games uh uh in Washington at one point and he's been around a lot of offenses and one thing that you see with veterans that have been around the league is like they they they start speaking football, you know, and and they may not know exactly what you call everything, but they're like, "Oh, nope. They call this that." And they already kind of have an idea what it looks like. And it's been it's been really great being in the room with those guys and and also listening to them support each other and help each other. >> Hey Clayton, Patrick Walk at dallascowboys.com. Uh as far as your backup running back battle is concerned. A lot of you know justifiable talk about Jayen Blue. Looks like he is taking those steps. He's starting to stack really good days. But Phil Mafa starting to surge a bit. Israel Abanaconda starting to kind of make some waves. And you know what you have in Malik Davis, aka the holiday killer, as Shotti calls him. How competitive can this backup running back competition be going forward? And how much fun is it for you as an offensive coordinator? >> Uh 100%. You know, I I think you're exactly right. The everybody in that room has done a really really good job. Um it has been a ton of fun to watch. And then the to me the the question of how competitive can it be is I don't know. Let's find out. Uh because all those guys are really doing a nice job. You know, Izzy made a really nice run yesterday where you you know, we've been talking to him about just being efficient, you know, not just running at the line of scrimmage and bending and cutting like how can I get in and out of a cut so that before it closes. Um we saw that from him yesterday. Malik just just keeps doing stuff right. And you know, the guy that probably doesn't get as much credit as he deserves right now is I think Phil Moff has had a really nice camp so far. And so, um, yeah, I mean, it's freaking battle it out, you know. Um, not not everybody's going to be on the team, so we got to we got to find a way to to figure out who's going to be able to separate themselves, and that room is extremely extremely competitive. >> Thanks, Brad Sham, Cowboys Radio 1053. The kind of along that line, in the tight end room, Clayton, it would appear that the Fant injury is going to open up some snaps for the two rookies over the next three weeks. what have you seen from those two guys and what you need to see from each of them going forward? >> I think they I think they both have um some real strengths. Uh you know, the last couple days I felt like we've seen DJ uh you know when we get in pads all of a sudden you go guy's guy's physical, you know, he's not he's not afraid to step and strike somebody. Um obviously with Trigg, you know, when he's in space, you see some things that not a whole bunch of dudes around the league can do. And so, um, the it's with the young guys, it is just constantly two steps forward, one step back. You think they got something, they don't, then you got to kind of retach it to them. Um, this is the second time they're hearing the install. I'm kind of a I'm a big proponent that the fourth time you hear an install is when you really figure it out.
