title: The Good and Not So Good from Day 7 of 49ers Training Camp
text: The 49ers just finished day seven of training camp. Here's who stood out. Keep in mind the following players did not participate. Nick Bosa, Dre Greenlaw, Osa Diggizua, Kyle Yuschek, Jacob Cowan, Carver Willis, Dejon Stribbling, and Kaylin Black. More on them in a minute. The good quarterback Brock Perie. He's by far the most physically gifted quarterback on the roster. Even though he's the smallest quarterback on the roster, he's just so quick and difficult to ca to contain in the pocket, which is important for the 49ers because they don't provide much of a pocket. And when it's time to throw, Pertie is making outstanding decisions with the ball. He hasn't forced a pass into coverage in more than a week. Unfortunately for him, his best receiver remains his running back and his best wide receiver currently is Jordan Watkins. Too bad the Niners alienated Brandon Iayuk by voiding his guarantees last year. Ply Pury really could use him. Running back Christian McAffrey. He hasn't missed a practice yet in camp. Suddenly, he's the most durable player on the team and he's still the Niners's best receiver. If he gets injured, they're screwed. They'd better be careful with him. And that includes Fred Warner, who threw a punch at McAffrey today. More on Warner in a minute. Left tackle Trent Williams. He participated in one-on- ones and 11on1vens, which is incredible for a 38-year-old future Hall of Famer. Williams hasn't practiced every day, but he has participated in roughly half the practices, as opposed to Nick Bosa, who has yet to take a snap in one-on- ones or 11on1vens. And yet, Bosa, who's 28, missed today's practice with soreness while Williams suited up and competed. That's one reason Williams is a future Hall of Famer and Bosa is not. Bosa doesn't play enough. More on him in a minute. Left guard Robert Jones. He took all the reps at left guard with the starters for the first time. If the coaches love secondyear guard Connor KBY, they wouldn't have given his reps to Jones today. This competition is wide open. Wide receiver Jordan Watkins. Now that Mike Evans, Ricky Pieraw, and Jacob Cowing are injured. The Niners top three healthy wide receivers in the depth chart are Demarcus Robinson, Debo Samuel, and Jordan Watkins. And today, the best of those three clearly was Watkins, who caught a deep touchdown pass from Pertie during 11on1vens. Of these three healthy wide receivers, Watkins is the youngest, the fastest, the quickest, and the best route runner. He can beat you with a quick slant or a post over the top. The only area of the field where he struggles is over the middle because he's not particularly big. Still, he's improving. Wide receiver Junior Bergen, he caught two passes from Pertie over the middle in the red zone. The second catch was a touchdown. Bergen is small, but he has been making a couple of plays every day and looks to have a good chance to make the team and return kickoffs along with Debo Samuel. The not so good defensive end Nick Bosa. He missed practice due to general soreness the day after a day off. Coming into today, the Niners had practiced just once in the previous three days and he still was sore even though he doesn't really practice. He warms up, he goes through the drills with his position and then watches his teammates compete during the one-on- ones and 11on1vens. Either he's protesting training camp's proximity to the to the electrical substation or he's really sore despite doing the absolute minimum the past two weeks. This has been the Niners's lightest training camp of the Kyle Shanahan era and yet the team still suffers three or four injuries a day. Maybe they should move training camp to a different site. It couldn't hurt. Defensive tackle Osa Odigizua. He also missed practice due to general sores. The Niners seem to shut down any player who has a hangail just so they can be on the field for week one. Unfortunately, these players aren't ready for live action and often get injured during the season. That's what happened to the Niners last year. Don't expect to see Odigizua on the practice field anytime soon. Same goes for Mike Evans and Dejon dribbling. Linebacker Dre Greenlaw. He also missed practice due to general soreness. At least he was on the field standing next to Raheem Morris in his stance taking mental reps. I never saw Bosa or Odigizua. Fullback Kyle Yuschek. He mispracticed with a broken finger. Hard to blame this one on the electrical substation. Maybe this injury is just a product of age. Use isn't exactly young. Linebacker Fred Warner. He practiced, which is commendable, but he tried to punch the ball out of McAffrey's hands during a run play, which is not smart. Warner already broke one running back's ribs in training camp by throwing a punch at the football. God forbid he injures McAffrey as well. Warner needs to chill out. He's playing like a rookie with something to prove. training camp in general, it's a joke. The Niners can't get anything meaningful done because every day another three or four players go down. I'm not saying the electrical substation is the reason for the injuries, but it could be. The Niners don't really know what effect that substation has on his players. Until they know for sure, or until they stop suffering so many injuries, they should move training camp somewhere else. Anywhere else. They could practice in my backyard if they'd like. Just get away from the giant electrical substation and replace the training staff that gets terrible grades from the players every year. And don't cancel mini camp and then throw your players into full speed practices during training camp with minimal ramp up. And don't sign older players with a history of injuries either. And don't rush injured players back onto the field before they're 100% healthy. I shouldn't have to remind the Niners of these things, but I will until something changes.

title: Brian Fleury: "We're All Continuing To Grow In The Right Direction" | Seattle Seahawks
text: How's everybody? Good. How are you? Great. >> Your first uh week plus of being the offensive coordinator here? >> Uh it's been great. I mean, obviously there's a good foundation here in place, a lot of good players. So, it's a exciting situation to walk into. It's been It's been awesome. >> What's the biggest change you've had to make going from a positional coach to a quarter? >> Uh obviously you're overseeing the entire group. Um, I'm used to installing into the entire group, but now just having to make sure that I'm paying attention to every aspect of every single drill. There are times as a position coach, you can kind of hunker down in your bunker and just focus on your own guys and and now I don't have that luxury anymore. >> Ryan, how much how much is installed right now and how much is still >> I would say a good chunk of the f the the foundation is installed. Uh, the challenge that we face is we're going against one style of defense every day and so much of the package is built to attack different styles of defense. So there's really no point in putting it in cuz it's not going to work or be executed properly against what we're seeing on a daily basis. But that's one of the reasons I'm excited to get to Tennessee and, you know, use some of those other pieces. >> So you'll roll some of that during the season, too, because you haven't seen those looks yet. >> Yeah, for sure. I mean, we'll find a way once we get into more like a controlled scout team period, we'll work on developing those skills before we get to that time. But for right now, we're just kind of focused on competing against each other, working on fundamentals, building the foundation, skills and effort and techniques and that sort of thing. How come how the the play calling aspects for you? Is there is that an adjustment at all from what you've been doing the last few years? >> Uh I I mean I've thought as a play caller for a long time. Obviously doing it for the first time at this level is going to present some challenges. Mike is doing a great job of like putting me through the ringer in terms of challenging situations. We go through different ones every day. For some reason we're always like down by a touchdown with 50 seconds left and no timeouts. I don't know who's burning through the timeouts, but it left it definitely like it helps me, you know, adjust to those situations. How much do you want to on offense dictate to a defense what you're going to do with your play calls versus put them in bad situations and and know that their rules you might want to break? >> Uh it's it's a combination of both. Uh it's really both kind of all the time. You know, we're attacking defenses and their structure. Um but utilizing our players in ways that fit their skill sets and and allow them to succeed. >> Ryan, you've obviously been in this division. You've known Cooper Cup and you've known his game for a long time, but working with him, what stands out being around him every day? Uh he just until you work in a building with him, you don't appreciate his love for every aspect of football. We've had so many conversations about how the O line is blocking run plays and things that are completely outside of the normal realm of his position group. So that's been really cool to experience and and I admire that >> a sequence or like a third and long conversion. The next play he's blocking on the edge. I mean is that pretty much sum up what? >> Yeah, I mean it does. We we were in a third and long situation and you know I saw them trying to sub. We wanted to get up on the ball quickly and he's like just such a versatile piece. He can do some of the things the tight ends do normally and uh having him out there is definitely makes it easy. >> When it comes to play call, is there ever a period where you're just literally practicing what you're saying? I mean, we talked to quarterbacks have to practice cadence and calling things, >> right? No, every day and and we're working through that. Um especially I try to make it harder on myself like go there's a lot of thought that will go into it beforehand going into a game. you'll have stuff kind of all laid out on your sheet, but I try and challenge myself at times to just think off the top of my head and and like see if I can get it out on time for the sake of the quarterbacks and the play call. And so we're we're practicing all the time. >> With all the the shifts and the motions and the time of the play clock that that takes up, does that like make it more important to be >> Yeah, if we're going to be able to utilize that part of the offense, we have to be able to get in and out of the huddle quickly. So, it definitely like they're aware of that and it's something we're working with. How's it been working with Justin Outton and Jake Pets uh with their continuity from last year to merging with you? >> Uh it's been great not only them but the entire coaching staff honestly like that you know it's the transition was very very easy. It took us a while in the offseason to get on the same page with just some differences in terminology and making sure that what a word you know I think one word means something and they think it means the exact same thing cuz sometimes you can get lost in translation across football cuz people recycle words. So that was a process but now that we've gotten back to camp and are installing things again it's it's been really awesome. Those guys have helped me a lot and you know I think we're all continuing to grow in the right direction. >> With the language, did you bring your language here or are you adapting to what they were doing? >> It's honestly a combination of both. Um there's I think the players have answered this question a lot and they're probably the best, you know, barometer as to where it stands. There's been a lot of continuity from a terminology standpoint in run game protections. There's a few things formation and motionwise that I've added and then they'd say it's probably 50/50 across the pass game. So, the guys that have been here, I think, have benefited from a little bit of the the same terminology. >> It's early, Brian, but how do you feel your blitz pickup, blitz recognition, blitz pickup, especially off the edge as much as Mike Sunzac? >> Yeah, I think it was pretty good today. We worked the drill specifically for that. I don't know what the the efficiency numbers were, but uh you know, I think Sam particularly does a great job of recognizing those things and getting us into the best possible scenario. >> You saw Sam down in San Francisco and now you're seeing him up here. Do you see a difference in in how he's playing now versus back then? [snorts] >> Well, there's a difference in his role and so, you know, he knew he was the backup and he was there helping support Brock and and his preparation maybe was a little bit different in that role than it is now. And now, you know, one of the first impressions I had when I got into the building is how much ownership he has over the entire thing. And wanted to know exactly what everybody's responsibilities were and how we were going to teach certain things. And then we've had a lot of great conversations about things he's done in the past in Minnesota and then here last year with Clint that, you know, I wasn't as familiar with, but we can find a way to implement because, you know, he executes it very at a high level. >> Where do you assess where the running game is right now in kind of the running backs today in Georgia? >> Uh, I I mean, I want it to be better. Um, but, you know, we're moving in the right direction. I think we've been efficient in practice, but uh, I see things through a different lens. It's not like the success of the play on the practice field. I'm just looking at everyone's alignment and the techniques, and there's there's a lot of room for growth there. Not to say that we're doing poorly, but you know, I expect that to be an extremely like reliable portion of our game, and it's it's not there yet. >> With all the ways that Mike's defense can put stress on offense, how does that help you as a play caller to to see that in practice? >> It definitely helps. I I think I think it's going to be more challenging. It's more challenging in practice than it will be in a lot of the games, you know, just with the the variety and the pressure packages and the movement and the physicality that they come with every single day. So, it's it's good to face that and then hopefully transition and when you're game planning and things are a little bit slowed down, a little bit more specific, it just makes it seem easier and slower for the players. >> How do you assess where Jaylen is in his development right now? >> Uh Jaylen's had, you know, a good week and a half. He had a really good offseason. He's had a good week and a half. He's doing a great job throwing the ball. I think statistically he's been really efficient passing the ball. um he's making plays with his feet when necessary, but we're really focused on him playing quarterback. And that that the elements of that aren't always visible to everybody. It's it's communication, it's timing, it's execution, it's efficiency, and he's really grown a lot in those areas. >> Dable said he saw your pickup truck in the parking lot. Maybe you like to run the football. Is that true? >> I like to run the football. I'm not sure what the the pickup truck has to do with that, but if that's the impression it gives, I'm okay with that. >> What have you done with the offensive line? and they coming back. What does that do for you as you try to create something? >> Yeah, it's an extremely rare situation, I think, to have all five starters returning, especially from a Super Bowl team. So, I'm walking into a really good situation. And then I've worked with John Benton before. He does a phenomenal job of coaching that group. So, the cohesion that they already have just makes it really, really easy to implement stuff. And then when you do realize that an adjustment needs to be made, they're just so used to working with each other and communicating that adjustments happen lightning fast. And so that that's a nice advantage to that situation. >> What is the importance of that ability to use two? >> Yeah, I I like using two backs because it can change the formation strength after the snap as opposed to the whole defense being able to identify it before the snap. Um, so I think it creates some fit problems and it's becoming less and less common across the league. So it means it's difficult more difficult to prepare for. So those are the elements I like about it. I think like you know I'm more of like an old school traditionalist just because of my upbringing in football and so I'm always going to want to play with two backs at some point and uh and I like the guys that we have in that role right now. >> To that end, how how are you at fullback? We know it's a situation but for what you want to install, you need to bolster that position. >> Uh I don't know that we need to bolster it. We're going to find creative ways to get a second back into the back field. It doesn't always have to be a traditional fullback. We've found ways to use receivers and lead blocking roles, other tight ends, even other running backs. So, we'll find a way to get it done with >> with Bill. Do you envision having like packages where he comes in the license? >> Uh, potentially. We'll see if if he's going to be active on game days, we're going to have ways to use his skills to our advantage um and surprise defenses with that. But, we have to, you know, his the decision about that is going to be based on how well he plays quarterback and we have to get over that hurdle first. >> Anything else, guys? Thanks. >> Thank you.

title: Mary Kay Cabot breaks down the Shedeur vs. Watson competition | Chris Simms Unbuttoned | NFL on NBC
text: We have a lot to talk about with Mary Kay. Hey, Mary Kay, how are you? >> I'm doing great, guys. How you doing? >> We're doing good. I'm glad you're out of the kitchen here to talk to us about some football and all of this. I I couldn't help it. I had to make that joke right there. All right. All right. But, um, thank you for joining us as always. We appreciate it. All right. >> Sure. >> Um, when you when you talk about right right off the bat, the QB competition, uh, it's is it's taking over the NFL. For your experience, you've been following the Browns forever. Okay. How does this compare to other Browns quarterback competitions you've been involved in? >> Well, I would say that this one is ratcheted up more than many of the others because of the Shador Sanders phenomenon. I've really never seen anything like it from a media standpoint. I've seen other very popular quarterbacks. I mean, you know very well, Chris, we had Johnny Manzel here and that was quite the circus. Uh, so I've been around uh those kinds of situations before, but just from an uh overall media standpoint, I think uh Shadore tops all of those because there's so much more social media now. Uh everyone now has an opinion. Every single time I turn on uh the internet or any kind of social media, you got someone else weighing in on who should be starting for the Cleveland Browns. So, it's pervasive. It's everywhere. And I think that's probably the biggest difference. That's that's crazy because I I that was going to be my next question. Mary Kay, how does this compare to Manzel Mania cuz that at the time that was the biggest thing in the sport. So that was kind of shocking for me to hear you just say that that you don't even think that compares to what we're seeing with Shadur right now. >> No, it doesn't. And like I said, it's because of just the the media power of this whole thing. And I mean the Sanders family themselves, they have their own media company and it has a lot of tentacles too. So there's just a lot uh that goes on here with this. And I think maybe had Johnny Manzel landed here in 2026, it would have been something similar to what we're seeing now with Shadore. So I think that's why uh you're seeing it everywhere because it's it's really a a a media thing. What do you think of the phenomenon of training camp stats every single day? And you get to see how fans react to them because we were talking about before you joined us, one guy on paper can have a really good day of practice, but when you're at practice every day, you might be like, well, he was going up against the third string or the second string or he was asked to make different throws and it gives the fans, it shapes the fans opinions in different ways. So, what do you think of this era we're in where that's become so popular? Well, you guys know as well as I do, it's pretty ridiculous to look at those numbers and think that uh they really impact what's going on on the field. First of all, you're talking about seven on sevens included in those numbers. Seven on sevens, what are you going to find out from seven on sevens? You will find out if somebody is accurate, but you're not going to find out if they can throw against a rush. You're not going to find out all these other things. you're not going to know if they can ID the defense or understand the play or get it called or slide the motions or the protections or do whatever you need to do. So, um so seven on sevens included in a quarterback tracker are in my opinion kind of a useless thing. If anything, uh I would think that you could do the quarterback tracker with pads on in an 11 on 111 drill. that would give you probably the the most accurate uh depiction of what you think is happening with the quarterback competition. But even then, here's what people seem to forget, and that is nobody knows how a quarterback is going to perform until you get into a live game situation. A defensive coordinator has game planned for you to take away your strengths. And uh you have to be out there trying to beat all of that, including the rush and all of the things that come with an NFL game. >> Yeah, that's right. I say that all the time. It's it's practice is nice and warm and cozy, but until you get out there and they can rip your head off and there's 70,000 fans screaming, you really don't know how the quarterback's going to handle that situation. And you made a lot of good points about seven on seven there. No. So, so now we're sitting here, you know, a little more than a week into training camp. if you had a feel for so far, right? You maybe other beat writers, what what's your feel about who's kind of leading the competition here through, you know, a little more than the first week of training camp? >> Well, first of all, there's still an install right now. Install ends on Thursday. And Todd Munin keeps on saying, "I'm not even really evaluating these guys right now. This is install. When we get done with install, then we will tailor the script to each quarterback. Each guy can go out there, play to his strengths a little bit more." And so right now, uh, it's apples to apples. There's divi they're dividing everything up. They're alternating days. I would say that Shadore has the momentum right now because he is making more explosive plays in practice. So, he's got the momentum, but you have to remember, we we're not sure would he have been sacked? Uh, you know, there's just so many things that go into it. But just in terms of actually completing passes, he definitely has the momentum and the edge right now. And it sort of was like that in mandatory mini camp as well. For some reason, uh, Deshawn didn't pop as much as he had earlier in OTAAS. And so right now, uh, I think even if you look at clips online and whatnot, you're seeing, uh, that it's heavy Shadore just in terms of who seems to be winning this competition. But there are other extenduating circumstances. I mean, we watched a practice the other day where, you know, it was a Mayday field goal situation and it didn't get executed correctly and Todd Monkin had some words with Shador and things like that. So, he's coming up the learning curve still just in terms of the overall operation of this offense, his second pro offense in two years. And Deshawn, uh, what he's not doing enough of, uh, is completing passes and making those explosive plays and hitting his targets on time and with rhythm and all that kind of stuff. So, these are the things that these two guys need to do. I wrote a column about this last night. If they want to pull ahead over the next couple weeks, Shadore has to just clean up the operation and keep coming up the learning curve in that way. And Deshawn needs to find more completions and he needs to find a rhythm. Now, it's been hard because they're not out there with all of their top receivers. You know, they're splitting these guys up. You know, two guys are on this field, two guys are on that field. So, they don't have the full complement of talent around them. We'll see how it goes over the next two weeks or so. >> Well, when you you know, when you you brought up the spring a little bit, and in the spring, it just seemed like the talk that was clearly Deshun Watson was in the lead, right? I mean, there was comments from everybody following the the whole situation about clearly it was Deshaawn Watson. Do you feel like it was clearly that or do you think it was a little bit of the Browns and Todd Monkin maybe trying to motivate Shadur a little bit to up his game or was it clearly just Deshaawn was the better one through the majority of the OTAAS? I think that Deshawn was so much further ahead just in terms of knowing the scheme, knowing, you know, being able to execute quarterback control, knowing what Todd Monin was going to want him to be doing at the line of scrimmage and all of those kinds of things. He was so much further ahead than Shadore at that point. Let's go back to uh a mini camp that they had, that extra bonus mini camp that they had in April. Uh Deshawn was clearly ahead and Shador had a long way to go, but you have to give him a ton of credit because he came bolting up that learning curve and he basically said, "I will not be denied. I'm staying in this quarterback competition." And he learned what he had to do to be able to function and operate effectively at the line of scrimmage. It's still a work in progress. You guys know what that's all about. And it takes time. I mean, he only started seven games last year, and once again, he's learning new terminology, new personnel, completely new offense. And some of the things that are happening in this offense, Deshawn executed under Bill O'Brien in Houston, and it's sort of that Tom Brady type of of >> carry over there, right? >> And and he he has that down. Uh but now he's got to put the other piece of it with it. And that is actually putting it out on the grass and and translating it to putting a drive together, making completions, and then ultimately scoring some points. >> I know it's early, but what's the notable difference between a Todd Monkin training camp and a Kevin Stansky >> Well, I would say the number one thing about Todd is that you know what he's thinking. You know how he feels about a situation. He's going to tell you a lot of things that Kevin never wanted to tell us. And that was just Kevin's style. We don't know if it's going to be better or worse. It's just different. Uh Todd wears his emotions on his sleeve. We hear him sometimes screaming at practice. We'll see him patting a guy on the back. And then uh you know in the press conferences he will give you something that you can use. And Kevin really never did that. Kevin never wanted to make a headline. Uh but Todd explains things. He tells us things. And I think it's a breath of fresh air for the fans and certainly uh members of the media. we have something that we can work with a little bit more. Let me give you an example real quick. I asked him the other day, how did he feel about Quinn Sean Judkins lighting up Mike Hall in a non-padded practice the other day? And Mike Hall was bent over and you know he he was not ready for uh you know just Quinn Sean blasting him. And Todd came out and said, "Hey, I talked to Quinn Sean about that already. Uh it was a mistake. It's the heat of the moment. You know, we don't define people by their mistakes. You know, he knows it was wrong." And it was just it was good information and we were able to illuminate some things in that regard. >> Todd Yeah, Todd is a so honest. That's what's awesome. Yeah, he is he's a straight shooter which is which makes him so fun to talk to all the time. So there's a part of me as we've heard this in football history before. >> We start the guy maybe we don't think should take over the team really in whole. Like there's a part of me that wonders, will Cleveland start Deshawn Watson week one knowing that they're going to bench him and put Shador Sanders in at some point? Uh but I guess the thing I I really want to ask you is do you think the Cleveland fan base is going to accept Deshun Watson being named the starter? I just feel like if it's not Shadura, they might pillage the streets and and you know try to take over the city of Cleveland. >> That is going to be a factor. That's definitely going to be a factor. And I think they even have to think about it uh as they dole out these preeason starts because they're going to need some data on how Deshawn is received in Huntington Bank Field and how he handles it if he gets booed, right? I mean, the last time he played here, uh there were some people cheering when he was down on the field with a ruptured Achilles. So, this is a very real situation that the Browns have to deal with that Deshawn is going to have to deal with. And if he has really good noiseancelling headphones, then, you know, maybe he's going to be okay. But mentally, mentally, he's going to have to be able to deal with this if he wants to be the starting quarterback of the Cleveland Browns. And you're right, this may be a situation where they're like, "Let's get Deshawn out there for the first how many ever games. See how it goes." know that we gave him a chance in the last year of his contract to see what he has and then maybe we turn it over to Shadore after he's had a little bit more time to assimilate the offense, get more up to speed at the line of scrimmage. See how that offensive line comes together with five new guys on it. See how those rookie quarter uh uh receivers come up the learning curve a little bit. let it kind of get going and gel and then put Shadore in when the offense has its act together a little bit more. If he went in there now and he's got, you know, a rookie left tackle and and they're worried about sliding protections and rookie receivers and things like that, that could be a tall order. So, these are all things that have to be considered. >> Yeah. We talk about it all the time. The team has to be ready to support the young quarterback, too. And I do think the coaches think of that, right? And that's a that's a big part of it. And I think it's a great point by you, Mary Kay, >> especially an old school coach. Yeah, you know, as we go back to so this quarterback competition overshadows a really good defense, a lot of talent at every single level of this defense, a defense now with no Miles Garrett. How does it feel out there? And how does the How different does it feel without him? Especially when you drop in still a young talented player like Jared Verse. >> Jared Verse has been a beast out here. I think he came in with a big chip on his shoulder and I really think that he's got a lot to prove and I think he's going to have a dynamite year for the Cleveland Browns. He's been spending this camp so far in the back field. He's he's been amazing. Now he does have to add to his pass rush repertoire. Uh he's just he's he's all power and that's great. Uh but now he needs to add to that a little bit and that's what these guys are going to try to coach him up on. I actually thought Javian Clowney would be really good for him if the Browns could have signed him because I think he would have helped him learn some of those other pass rush moves and whatnot. Uh, so Jared needs to finish more than he has so far. But just from a power standpoint, I'll tell you what, I mean, these guys are feeling it. Spencer Fono, the rookie left tackle, Dewan Jones, who's just a man mountain. I mean, these guys are feeling uh the impact of Jared verse. The other thing about Jared Ve that I think is very important, he's a force multiplier. He's a unifier. He brings guys together. He's a guy's guy. Guys are going to be hanging out at his house and vice versa. And Miles wasn't necessarily like that. Uh Miles would leave here and kind of go off and do his own thing. Uh he didn't live, breathe, sleep, eat football. And uh you know, so I I just think that in some ways Jared Vers is going to be good for this team. And I also think they'll spread the wealth a little bit. They're still going to be a good defense. That's if you're a Browns fan, that's great to hear because Verse could have taken this trade one of two ways where you go from I'm on the edge of I'm on a Super Bowl contender and now I go to Cleveland who's in an interesting place, but instead as she's alluding to, he's embraced it and kind of run with more of a leadership. >> That's why people love them coming out in the draft because of the personality. All right, so you brought up the two young receivers. You got two receivers in the top 39 picks of the draft. give us just a little bit of the feel so far through camp with Casey Conception and Denzel Boston and kind of how that's going and who's impressed there. >> These guys are going to be really good. They've already had really good springs and really good camps. Now Casey right now is nursing a little bit of a sore shoulder. He came down hard on it in practice the other day. Uh gave everybody a little bit of a scare, so he rested yesterday, but he should be okay with that. uh what he showed is that shiftiness, that agility, that ability to uh to separate and get the run after catch. So uh he brings that speed element to the table and you know sort of the you know Z Flowers light type of situation and then you've got Denzel Boston who is 6'4 215 and he's been catching everything that comes his way. Now, he's not the speediest guy, but he's going to win that 50/50 ball and uh and he spends a ton of time on the Jugs, and he's been really, really good in this camp. I would say he's probably been the best receiver in this camp, the most explosive plays, the most standout receiver uh in this camp so far. I think these guys are really going to elevate this receiving core, which this team really needed. >> Oh, that that's good to hear. I love Denzel Boston coming out, so that would be nice for me. All right, one more question. I know you have to go, but I have to ask this. you you did have Dion Sanders there uh a few days ago. He was there. And I guess what I want to know is just how was how did you feel that was received within the organization? Maybe guys in the locker room just the the general conversation around it? Did it look odd, you know, that a guy, you know, the dad in the quarterback competition of course is there and it seems like he's hovering. You know what? How did it come off to you, Mary Kay? Well, you know, when you have someone uh as accomplished and famous as Dion Sanders, there are a different set of rules. Todd Monkin was very excited to have him here. He spent time talking to him about Shadore. He was more than willing to do that. And of course, Dion, I'm sure, really appreciated that. And then, you know, he just sat quietly at the top of the bleachers. He did have his white cowboy hat on. So, you know, none of us wear cowboy hats to practice. So, um and it was not a fan day. It was a day that there were no fans out here. So, you know, he he did stand out a little bit up there at the top of the bleachers, but he didn't do any media. He didn't talk to anybody. He didn't try to be intrusive. Uh he just sat there watching his son, evaluating him, critiquing him, and then he spent time with Shadore afterwards. It was not intrusive. It was not invasive. It was perfectly fine. And like I said, I mean, he's different. It's Dion. It's so it's perfectly okay. He talked to Andrew Barry and and I don't think it it turned practice into a circus or anything like that. >> No, it didn't seem it didn't seem it. That that's that's cool. That's good to hear. That's what it seemed like. That's what I thought you might say. I just wanted to make sure there, too, because we know it's it's sensitive when it comes to quarterback competitions and people look into everything. Mary Kay, you're a legend. We really appreciate you coming on here, hanging out. We might call you again in a few weeks, maybe when a decision's made, we're getting close. You need to update us, okay?
